cues.text: A Host That Would Not Fall
On Easter Sunday, 1254, at the church of St. Amatus in Douai , in northern France, a priest distributing Holy Communion accidentally dropped a consecrated Host toward the floor.
Tradition holds that before it could land, the Host rose back up on its own and came to rest gently on the corporal spread beneath the paten, in full view of the congregation.
Word of the sign reached Thomas de Cantimpré , a Dominican friar, doctor of theology, and suffragan Bishop of Cambrai.

He traveled to Douai to examine the matter personally and later recorded his own testimony in his theological work Bonum universale de Apibus : "I saw the face of Christ crowned with thorns, with two drops of Blood."
A Devotion That Outlived a Revolution
By 1356, just a century after the event, the church of St. Amatus was already keeping a regular weekly devotion to the relic.
The church itself was destroyed during the French Revolution , but not before a canon of the collegiate church of St. Peter, sensing the danger, removed the Host and placed it in a small wooden box.
He hid it beneath the Altar of the Dead, leaving with it a note in Latin identifying the relic for whoever might one day find it.
The box remained hidden for over sixty years, until 1854, when the pastor of St. Peter's discovered it during work beneath the altar.
Inside was a small Host, still white, together with the canon's original note dated January 5, 1793.
The note asked that the relic be preserved for the faithful of the future.
The Host remains venerated today at the Collegiate Church of St. Peter in Douai.
The faithful still gather there every Thursday of the month in prayer before it.
By the town's own reckoning, this devotion has survived a medieval accident, a revolution, and sixty years of quiet concealment beneath an altar built for the dead.
